articles.title: How these notes age
articles.summary: Publication, editing, review, and expiry are different events. Here is how to read their dates.
articles.author: Jean Marin

visual.title: Three different clocks
visual.caption: An edit changes the edit date. Only a technical review changes the review date. Neither resets the age of a news report.

sections.title: News has a defined lifetime
paragraphs: News and magazine editions describe information available at a known time. After three calendar months, the site labels them Outdated news and moves them out of the current listing. The archive remains accessible.
A later edit does not renew that news window. A materially new report gets a new dated entry and links to the earlier one.

sections.title: Guides need review
paragraphs: A guide explains knowledge that can remain useful for longer. Its last technical review and next review date are visible. The default proposed review period is six months. Fast-changing instructions use three months.
Review due means the planned check has not been recorded. It does not prove the content is wrong. Known errors require an immediate correction or warning.

sections.title: Experiments keep their context
paragraphs: An experiment is a record of one test setup. It keeps the test date, product versions, method, results, and limitations. A dated result does not guarantee the same behavior in a newer release.

visual.title: The release path

sections.title: A test, not a research article
paragraphs: This page tests the publication process. It contains no private research or client material. The current release marker is publication-test-v2. The first public release used publication-test-v1 and was checked before this update.

sections.title: What the check covers
paragraphs: The first stage checks that this page is accessible at its public address. A second release changes the marker. Reading the changed public page checks that updates also reach the website.
The catalogue and maintenance ledger are generated from the same article metadata. Every public page includes an explanatory visual.

articles.title: Quantization: how a model fits in less memory
articles.summary: Quantization stores model weights with fewer bits. This guide shows how groups and scales work, what 4-bit really costs, and what is lost.
articles.author: Jean Marin

visual.title: One group of weights in three steps, and model size at three precisions
visual.caption: Quantization stores each weight as a small integer plus one scale shared by the group. The group shrinks from 128 to 48 bits, and the restored values differ slightly from the originals. At scale, a 7-billion-weight model drops from 14.00 GB (16 bits per weight) to 3.72 GB (4.25 bits per weight). The weights are invented numbers for teaching, not from a real model. The 8-weight group is a stand-in; real groups are larger (for example 64). The same example is worked in the article text.

articles.title: A small test of code graphs: no help on easy questions, a hint on a hard one
articles.summary: Nine runs, three setups, one small codebase. A code graph did not help on easy questions and may have helped on one hard question. A lead, not a result.
articles.author: Jean Marin
articles.tested_note: Exact run dates not recorded; runs fell between 2026-11-13 and 2026-11-17 (inferred). 2026-11-17 is the upper bound.
articles.versions: Entire CLI 0.12.2; entire-graph 0.6.0 (no-egress on); graphify 0.9.108 (tree-sitter only); agent model set to automatic, not identified
articles.method: Three setups (agent alone, with entire-graph, with graphify), same model setting (automatic selection; actual model may differ between runs) and prompts, fresh context, graph setups told to prefer the graph. Three tasks (two small, one long), one run each, nine runs. Answers scored against a hidden facts checklist by a judge designed not to see the setup (judge model not recorded). Measured credits, peak context, turns, elapsed time.
articles.limitations: n=1 per setup per task; three of nine tasks run; one small private, mostly Python repository; model setting automatic (actual model may differ between runs) and judge model not recorded; run dates inferred; no token counts; credits are platform-specific; newer tool releases may exist.

visual.title: Credits, seconds and turns per setup, one run each
visual.caption: Small pilot, not a benchmark: one run per setup per task, nine runs. All nine answers were correct. Credits, seconds and turns are shown as measured. Differences may be noise.
